HSCT engines will have much higher jet exhaust speeds compared to today's subsonic airliners.
Jet noise, caused by the turbulent mixing of high-speed exhaust with the surrounding air, poses a significant challenge for HSCT engine designers.
HSCT engines use advanced mixer-ejector nozzles to entrain and mix large quantities of ambient air with the jet stream, reducing noise to airport noise certification levels.
As the HSCT gains speed and climbs, poor ejector inlet recovery and ejector ram drag contribute to poor thrust, making it advantageous to turn off the ejector.
Turning off the ejector prematurely can cause unacceptable noise levels to propagate to the ground, even when the aircraft is many miles from the airport.
The optimizer dynamically chooses the best altitude-velocity path and throttle setting history to minimize the noise propagated to the ground.
High altitudes are desirable to reduce noise, but the HSCT can either climb quickly to high altitudes using a high, noisy throttle setting or climb more slowly at a lower, quieter throttle setting.

The noise metrics used in the calculations are based on recommendations from researchers at NASA Langley, who have correlated the flyover noise annoyance levels of actual laboratory subjects with a variety of noise measurements.
The HSCT's climb noise is characterized by relatively low noise levels, long durations, and low-frequency spectra.
Analysis of the data from the optimizer has shown that significant reductions in noise may be obtained with trajectory optimization.
Only small penalties in HSCT range or fuel performance occur since the throttling operations are performed in the subsonic portion of the climb path where thrust is plentiful.
